Written by KARI PAUL

Starting this week, dozens of people will pull out $20 bills to find the White House on the back submerged in water: a striking image that comes as part of a new call to action over climate change.

The project is the last of three “currency interventions” by San Francisco-based artist Joseph DeLappe. In the past, he has call​ed attention to drone warfare and police brutality with similar projects.

WAVE DOLLAR

Photo: Joseph DeLappe

As part of this campaign, he created more than 100 stamps of a waterline, representing the rising sea levels caused by climate change. He has distributed 50 so far to people across the US. DeLappe said through the project, he aims to change the way people look at money.

“The sea level rising stamp is a way to put a graphic image of sea level rising on currency,” he said. “I wanted to think of cash as a type of visual, public space and create this participatory moment with volunteers from all over. It's as much about people stamping as the people who will eventually see the cash."

In addition to the recipients of the original stamps, those interested in volunteering can request additional stamps on DeLappe’s website.

Delappe’s first dollar-defacing project distributed stamps of drones in order to bring drone warfare overseas to the attention of more Americans. Hundreds of people requested stamps, he said, and there are now at least 750 drone-stamped bills in circulation today.

DeLappe said climate change is increasingly at the heart of his work.

“In my work as an artist and activist, I think a lot about what I want to spend my time and energy focused on: What are the larger issues facing us?” he said. “The environmental issues right now are some of the biggest challenges facing the planet. That’s something I’m going to start focusing on more and more, because in this case time is of the essence. It’s very serious to all of us.”

Volunteers interested in participating in the project can order a ​stamp through DeLappe’s website and upload photos of stamped bills there.

I guess I'm thinking long-term, but upvotes and downvotes are a terrible way to judge the worth of a comment.

While they are helpful if etiquette is followed in determining whether a comment is on topic, reading comments in larger threads become a chore.

The solution is often to moderate more vigorously, but if the goal of voat is to promote free speech, there needs to be a programmatic solution that allows users to self-curate comments; without always relying on a governing body of moderators in each subverse determining whether a comment should remain or not.

As a result, I would recommend that instead of relying purely on upvotes or downvotes, we allow users to tag the comments of other users premised on a variety of possible types. While I don't have a solid idea of which specific tags to use, a few examples of comment tags that could be considered can include:

  • Funny

  • Insightful (ie, the commenter brings new information or understanding to the topic)

  • Creative

  • Shitpost (sometimes you want shitposts & dank memes, and sometimes those shitposts can be quality content too)

  • High Quality

  • Low Effort

Users who come into threads can then filter comments based on tags. Given the goal of voat, this can make it easier to determine the quality of content if the goal is to compensate users.

There can also be thread-specific tags that can be used. While sorting by flair is useful, an interesting way to promote quality content is to allow for the sorting of all threads on voat (that choose to be included) premised on universal tags. This way, from the get go, you can click on a universal tag from the homepage or the top bar if you want to find original content. Having a "repost" tag (with an option to post a link to the repost) can help filter away repeat content.

Now, all of this begs the question: what would be the threshold for a comment tag in order for it to be considered "funny", "insightful", or "creative"? A solution for this would be to:

  • Allow a 1 comment to many tags relationship. Logically, a comment can be both funny and insightful.

  • Sort comments by the number of times tagged. This would be the simplest way to sort things out and would be less of a programming hassle.

I wouldn't say to remove upvotes or downvotes (perhaps on voat they can denote quality, where upvotes are "high" and downvotes are "low), but I would argue that allowing tags and filtering content by tags can make it an easier user experience, while creating an environment that encourages the creation of content that fulfills the tags' demands. Finally, it would make user profiles more interesting: people can end up as ranked "Most Insightful on /v/CommunityName" or even ranked "Top Shitposter on /v/CommunityName". It would definitely serve as a differentiation factor that would make voat distinct from reddit/digg style binary "upvote versus downvote" sites.
